paper_metadata.title: Knowledge-Based Weak Supervision for Information Extraction of Overlapping Relations
paper_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the 49th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2011)
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper presents MULTIR, a knowledge-based weak-supervision, multi-instance learning approach for extracting overlapping relations. It combines sentence-level extraction with corpus-level aggregation, learns from Freebase matched to New York Times text, and reports accuracy gains and fast execution at aggregate and sentence levels.

problem_addressed: Learn relation extractors from a structured database and unstructured text without manually labelled sentences, while overcoming noisy heuristic database-text matches and the incorrect assumption that one entity pair can have only one relation. The target is binary relation extraction from New York Times sentences, including overlapping Freebase relations for the same entity pair.

secondary_families: Joint entity-relation extraction (including joint triple extraction)
methodology.description: MULTIR groups all sentences containing an entity pair. For every candidate relation it creates a Boolean corpus-level fact variable Y^r, so multiple relations may simultaneously be true; each sentence has a latent label Z_i in the relation set plus none. Relation-sensitive lexical, POS, named-entity, and dependency-path features score sentence labels. Deterministic OR join factors require every positive aggregate fact to be expressed by at least one sentence. Weak labels are relation bit-vectors obtained from Freebase facts for matched entity pairs. Training uses online, Viterbi-approximated hidden-variable perceptron updates: compare an unconstrained best assignment with the best latent sentence assignment consistent with database labels and update their feature difference. At prediction, unconstrained sentence labels are independently selected and induce aggregate facts; label-constrained training inference is reduced to weighted edge cover and greedily approximated in O(|R|·|S|). This is relation extraction rather than joint entity-and-relation extraction: entity mentions and their matching to Freebase are preprocessing inputs.

ontology_or_schema_use.value: Freebase supplies the closed inventory of relation names R and atomic binary facts Δ used as weak aggregate labels. Its entity names are also used to match detected text phrases. The paper does not perform ontology discovery; Freebase is an external schema/knowledge-base constraint for supervision and output relation labels.

input_output.input_type: Unstructured New York Times news-text sentences, preprocessed into sentences containing two phrases matched to Freebase entities; training additionally uses Freebase binary facts and relation names.
input_output.input_granularity: Sentence-level relation mentions grouped as a bag/set of all sentences that co-mention an entity pair; the model assumes both entity mentions are noun phrases in one sentence.
input_output.output_representation: Canonical binary ground relation facts r(e1,e2) over Freebase relation names; for sentential extraction, a mapping Γ from each extracted fact to the set of corpus sentences that express it. Multiple relation facts may share the same entity pair.

evaluation.setting: The authors follow Riedel et al. (2010) for weak-supervision data generation, features, and aggregate evaluation. They train with 50 iterations, selected in development experiments. Aggregate evaluation compares extracted relations with Freebase and is acknowledged to underestimate accuracy because the knowledge base is incomplete. Sentential performance is manually assessed on a 1,000-sentence sample; relation-specific estimates manually inspect 100 sampled sentences from each of two sets per relation. The paper notes that this sampled sentential design can overestimate recall because unpredicted sentences are not manually checked.

value: MULTIR achieved competitive or higher aggregate precision over nearly all recall levels and extended maximum aggregate recall from 20% to 25% with little precision loss versus the compared Riedel approach.

At the highest reported sentential-recall point, MULTIR achieved 72.4% precision, 51.9% recall, and F1=60.5%; its sentential precision–recall curve had higher recall than SOLOr while retaining high precision.
When overlap was not modeled in the restricted training condition, average precision increased by 12 points but recall fell by 26 points and F1 fell from 60.5% to 40.3%.

MULTIR required about one minute to train and under one second to test, compared with about six hours training and four hours testing for the Riedel et al. approach on the stated NY Times splits, excluding preprocessing.

value: Author claim: Unlike the compared multi-instance model, the separate Boolean aggregate variables permit overlapping relations for one entity pair while retaining sentence-level predictions.
Experimental result: It improves recall at aggregate and sentential levels relative to the reimplemented comparator and provides a direct sentence justification for extracted facts.
Experimental result: The deterministic-OR decomposition gives markedly faster training and test time in the reported comparison.

Review-level inference: The output is especially useful for knowledge-base population because each canonical relation fact can be associated with supporting source sentences rather than only a corpus-level label.

value: Author-reported empirical observation: Relation-specific recall is consistently low and performance is best only where there are sufficiently many true weak-supervision matches.
Author-reported empirical observation: Some relation overlaps produce nearly all false weak labels; the administrative-divisions relation could not be learned accurately.

Review-level inference: The approach depends on upstream named-entity recognition and string/name matching to Freebase, while the model assumes an oracle for entity mentions and does not normalize or disambiguate them itself.

Review-level inference: The model is limited to binary relations with both entity mentions appearing as noun phrases in one sentence; it therefore does not address cross-sentence, n-ary, or event extraction in this paper.

Author-identified: Extending the weakly supervised learning framework beyond relation extraction to coreference and named-entity classification remains future work.
